steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA) are both long chain polymers of nucleotides, but they differ in several fundamental ways that give each molecule distinct chemical properties and biological roles:

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   The extra hydroxyl group in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
   Uracil pairs with adenine during RNA base‐pairing.

3. Strandedness and structural form  
   • DNA: Usually double-stranded, forming a right-handed double helix with complementary base pairing (A–T, G–C).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded, but can form complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops, double helical regions) through intramolecular base pairing.

4. Stability  
   • DNA: Chemically more stable (deoxyribose + double helix protects bases). Can persist for the lifetime of the cell or organism.  
   • RNA: More prone to hydrolysis (extra –OH) and degradative enzymes (RNases); typically shorter-lived.

5. Function  
   • DNA: Long-term storage of genetic information; template for its own replication and for RNA synthesis.  
   • RNA: Multiple roles—messenger RNA (mRNA) carries coding instructions to ribosomes; transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are integral to translation; microRNA, siRNA, and others regulate gene expression; some RNA molecules possess catalytic activity (ribozymes).

6. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined mostly to the nucleus in eukaryotes (plus mitochondria and chloroplasts); circular chromosomes in the nucleoid region of prokaryotes.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) but functions largely in the cytoplasm; also found in nucleolus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, and other RNA granules.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA is replicated by DNA polymerases into more DNA.  
   • RNA is synthesized (transcribed) from DNA by RNA polymerases; except in RNA viruses, which may copy RNA from RNA.

8. Length and copy number  
   • DNA molecules are very long, encompassing entire chromosomes, and only two copies per diploid cell.  
   • RNA molecules are typically much shorter (from <100 nt tRNAs to several kilobases mRNAs) and produced in many copies as needed.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA is actively repaired by sophisticated systems (mismatch repair, excision repair, recombination repair).  
   • RNA generally is not repaired; damaged RNA is usually degraded and resynthesized.

10. Chemical modification  
    • DNA: Methylation (e.g., 5-methylcytosine) used in epigenetic regulation.  
    • RNA: Wide variety of base and sugar modifications (pseudouridylation, methylation, etc.), especially in tRNA and rRNA, affecting stability and function.

In summary, DNA is the stable, double-stranded repository of genetic information, whereas RNA is typically a transient, single-stranded working copy used in gene expression, regulation, and catalysis.
